evidence.title: AUGUR-AI: a real-time artificial intelligence interpreter for indocyanine green fluorescence angiography in colorectal surgery
evidence.outcome: ICGFA interpretation model IOU on unseen videos from other surgeons, institutions and imaging systems
evidence.effect: Test IOU 0.62 on held-out same-institution data fell to 0.45 on 15 additional unseen videos, with no prediction for one poor-perfusion case.
evidence.quote: Further ICGFA model testing on 15 additional unseen videos returned IOU = 0.45 with, importantly, no prediction when classifying one case of poor perfusion.

evidence.title: Consensus, dissensus and synergy between clinicians and specialist foundation models in radiology report generation
evidence.effect: 55.4% ICU; 77.7% outpatient; 94% no abnormal findings preferable/equivalent by half or more of panel.
evidence.quote: We observe a wide distribution of preferences across the panel, ranging from full consensus to dissensus, across clinical settings and regions, with 55.4% of Flamingo-CXR intensive care reports evaluated to be preferable or equivalent to clinician reports, by half or more of the panel, rising to 77.7% for outpatient x-rays overall and to 94% for the subset of cases with no pertinent abnormal findings.
evidence.sample_unit: certified radiologists evaluating AI-generated and human-written chest radiograph reports

evidence.title: Assessing the Safety and Clinical Appropriateness of Breast Cancer Advice From Consumer-Grade Large Language Models
evidence.venue: Journal of medical imaging and radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Clinical appropriateness of LLM answers with WA-specific terminology versus general questions
evidence.effect: Appropriate answers: ChatGPT 97%, Perplexity 90%, Gemini 87%. Inappropriate responses were more common with WA-specific terminology, particularly for Perplexity and Gemini.
evidence.quote: Inappropriate responses were more common when questions included WA-specific terminology, particularly for Perplexity and Gemini.

evidence.title: Predicting Momentary Suicidal Ideation From Smartphone Screenshots Using Vision-Language Models: Prospective Machine Learning Study
evidence.outcome: Generalization of performance to unseen individuals
evidence.effect: Subject holdout AUC≈0.50 (near chance); a simple lexical screening method retained modest discrimination (AUC=0.62).
evidence.quote: Subject holdout generalization was near chance (AUC≈0.50), though a simple lexical screening method retained modest discrimination (AUC=0.62).

evidence.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models in Infectious Disease Decision-Making: From Examination to Clinical Practice
evidence.effect: TB errors exceeded 60% for Gemini 14/21 (66.7%), ChatGPT-5 17/26 (65.4%), and Grok 3 16/25 (64.0%); DeepSeek 7/16 (43.8%).
evidence.quote: Except for DeepSeek-R1 (7/16, 43.8%) and doctors (12/24, 50.0%), tuberculosis-related errors exceeded 60% of total errors in most LLMs trained primarily on Western corpora, including Gemini 2.5 Flash (14/21, 66.7%), ChatGPT-5 (17/26, 65.4%), and Grok 3 (16/25, 64.0%) ( Figure 2 ; Supplementary Table 12 in Supplementary material 5 ).

evidence.title: CrossMed: A Multimodal Cross-Task Benchmark for Compositional Generalization in Medical Imaging
evidence.outcome: Performance on unseen modality-anatomy-task combinations versus seen combinations
evidence.effect: Related-split models reached 83.2% classification accuracy and 0.75 segmentation cIoU; performance dropped significantly under Unrelated and zero-overlap conditions.
evidence.quote: Models trained on Related splits achieve 83.2 percent classification accuracy and 0.75 segmentation cIoU, while performance drops significantly under Unrelated and zero-overlap conditions, demonstrating the benchmark difficulty.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Cardiac Function Estimation from Phone Videos of Echocardiograms
evidence.outcome: LVEF estimation accuracy on phone-recorded videos versus native DICOM
evidence.effect: MAE worsened from 6.08 to 7.00 percentage points, R² decreased from 0.60 to 0.49, and AUC decreased from 0.93 to 0.91
evidence.quote: Without phone-video fine-tuning, the primary model achieved a mean absolute error of 7.00 percentage points, coefficient of determination of 0.49, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.91 on phone-recorded videos; corresponding native DICOM performance was 6.08 percentage points, 0.60, and 0.93, respectively.

evidence.title: PORTRAIT: a calibrated patient ‘Passport’ with built-in refusal - describing individuals against a reference population
evidence.effect: Two transfer tests returned negatives; ocular transfer did not hold coverage at thin-n.
evidence.quote: Two transfer tests returned negatives; the ocular transfer did not hold coverage at thin-n.

evidence.title: Robustness evaluation of deep neural networks for endoscopic image analysis: Insights and strategies
evidence.outcome: Performance loss from domain gap between development data and real-world endoscopic images
evidence.effect: Domain gap between high-quality development images and clinical input produced an 11.6% (±1.5) performance decline under calibrated degradations.
evidence.quote: This so-called domain gap between the data used for developing the system and the data it encounters after deployment, and the impact it has on the performance of deep neural networks (DNNs) supportive endoscopic CAD systems remains largely unexplored.
evidence.sample_unit: prospectively collected low-quality endoscopic images (plus public KVASIR-SEG and GIANA images)

evidence.title: Out-of-Distribution Detection as a Risk-Control Strategy for Medical Classification Machine Learning Models
evidence.effect: OOD AUROC often fell below 0.5, indicating some test subpopulations were worse than random despite acceptable global performance.
evidence.quote: Indeed, for a few of the OOD detectors, the OOD AUROC often fell below 0.5, indicating that these algorithms found test observation sub‐populations where the clinical classifier was on average worse than random.
evidence.sample_unit: patients/samples across three datasets (1081 dermoscopy images; 1034 transcriptomic samples; 2804 participants)
evidence.country: USA (multi-country datasets: ISIC from MSKCC and international centers; malaria from multiple countries incl. Myanmar; mPower)

commentary.bottom_line: Seven sources endorse documenting context of use, sources of setting variation, dataset constraints, and limits on generalization, but no study has tested whether such documentation prevents performance failures in new settings. Ten hazard studies show that performance often drops when models meet data, sites, or populations that differ from development data.

perspectives.view: No study tests whether documenting context of use changes outcomes, so certainty about the practice is rated as no direct evidence. Nine of the ten hazard studies are level 4 or 5 offline or benchmark designs, and one is a level 3 deployment study. They consistently show performance loss outside development conditions. That establishes the problem but does not show the remedy works.

Aggregate metrics can hide subgroup failures. OOD AUROC often fell below 0.5 for some subpopulations despite acceptable global performance. A surgical imaging model's IOU fell from 0.62 to 0.45 on unseen videos, and it gave no prediction for one poor-perfusion case. Documented limits may help users recognize out-of-scope use, though no study confirms this.

Inputs captured in routine workflow differ from development data. Phone-recorded echocardiogram videos raised LVEF error from 6.08 to 7.00 percentage points, and low-quality endoscopic images produced an 11.6% performance decline. These results suggest documentation should describe expected input quality and capture methods. No study has examined whether clinicians read and act on such statements.

Local terminology and regional disease patterns affected accuracy. LLM answers were more often inappropriate when questions used Western Australia-specific terms. Tuberculosis error rates exceeded 60% for three models tested on Chinese clinical cases. No study examined Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy settings, so documented contexts of use may omit populations that differ from development data.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks for instructions on preparing input data and on the expected characteristics of users. FUTURE-AI asks for a standard definition of the clinical task. These endorsements rest on expert consensus. No study shows that labeling of this kind reduces generalization failures after deployment.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without documented context of use and generalization limits. A useful test would measure whether such documentation changes local validation decisions, reduces out-of-scope use, or improves site-level performance. It should include safety-net and limited English proficiency settings.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard study (pmid:42311928) used Chinese clinical cases in a non-English context and found region-specific error patterns. This suggests that context-of-use statements may not describe these populations unless developers report them explicitly.
